The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

James turns his shoulder to the barrel. The cards keep slapping behind him, *find the lady, friends*, and he stops listening.

The cat answers through the bond the way it always does, in pieces rather than words:

*A man. In the dark between the shut stalls. Still. Watching the barrel-man's hands. Not you.*

Then, sharper, with the feeling of fur rising along a spine:

*The barrel smells wrong. The little coins. Wet stone. Old candles. I don't like it.*

James lets his eyes drift down the bridge, the way a bored man looks around in a queue. Between the two shuttered stalls the lamplight gives out, and a young man leans in the gap with his hood up and his arms folded. He isn't looking at the queue or the river. Every time silver crosses the barrel his lips move a little, like someone keeping count. Then he goes still again.

The drover in front of James pays his toll and moves on. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

James gives his name and his business. Sergeant Marrow writes it without looking up. *WORGEN* goes on the chalkboard in square capitals, and she copies it into a ledger lying open at her elbow. The page is full of names in a cramped hand. A few of them, here and there down the column, have a small chalk cross beside them.

At *the bed first* the chalk stops. She looks up, gives him one slow look from his face to his cloak, and isn't charmed.

"Everyone wants the bed first." Her eyes stay on the cut of the old regimental cloak a moment longer. "Tethyr?"

She holds her inky palm out flat over the trestle without waiting for the answer.

"Two copper, on foot. The cat's free."

James counts the two coppers into her palm. Her fingers close over them, and the coins go into a tin box under the trestle without her looking.

"Tethyr. Infantry, then scouts."

"Hm." It's the closest she's come to approving of anything all evening. She writes something short beside *WORGEN* in the ledger. He can't read it upside down in this light.

When he lowers his voice and mentions the man between the stalls, she doesn't turn her head. Her eyes go past James's shoulder, across the barrel, into the dark gap, and come back. Fifteen years of not being caught looking.

"Then he's counting for somebody. On this bridge, somebody's usually the Guild." She wipes the chalk off her thumb onto her sleeve. "Not my business until somebody bleeds."

"The game's been there since the thaw. Every evening, same barrel, he pays his pitch like the fishwives do." She stops, as if weighing whether the next part is worth saying to a stranger. "He pays out more than you'd think. People walk away from that barrel with coppers in their hands, grinning."

Her gaze drops to the open ledger for a moment. Down the column, past a dozen names, her eye stops on one of the little chalk crosses and stays there a beat too long. Then she shuts the book over her inky fingers. It isn't quite a slam.

"Lower City gate's at the north end, past Wyrm's Rock. Shuts at the last bell, so if you want a bed inside the walls, don't stand about. There are rooms on the bridge if you don't mind the river under your floor." She looks past him at the cart waiting in line. "Next."

Behind James the cards slap down on the barrel again. *Find the lady.* A drover laughs, and the copper clinks as it's paid out.

At his heel the cat's ears flatten for a moment at the sound, then come up again.

James steps past the trestle and out of the line. The press of carts pulls toward the north end of the bridge, and he lets it go by. He stops at the railing, where the river runs black under the boards and smells of tar and something rotting in the reeds. From here the barrel is about thirty feet off. That's close enough to see the hands and far enough to be just another tired traveller resting his feet.

The cat leaves his heel without a sound. It goes the long way round, past a cart wheel and behind a fishwife's basket, and sits down among the drovers' boots as if it has always lived there.

Dov Penhallow has a new customer, a broad drover with a sunburned neck and a silver piece already on the barrelhead. The cards go face up so he can see the lady, then face down. Dov's hands start moving.

James doesn't have to try hard to read it. It's like reading a page in a language he grew up in. Dov's patter is good and his fingers are better. On the third pass the switch is right there under his right hand: the loose grip, the lift that lets the lady slide one card over. A sharp makes that move without thinking. Dov doesn't make it. The lady stays where the drover's eyes have been following her the whole time. Dov threw the game, and he threw it cleanly enough that nobody but another card man would see it.

The drover slaps the middle card and the lady turns over. The drovers around him whoop.

The payout is the second thing James sees. The silver stake goes into Dov's waistcoat pocket with the others. The winnings don't come from there. Dov reaches to his left hip, to a small, dark leather purse on its own thong, and counts out coppers. James makes it ten or a dozen. The purse is pulled shut again at once. Dov hands the coppers across with the drover's silver on top and says "Well played, friend, well played." The two purses never touch.

Between the shuttered stalls, the hooded young man's lips moved when the silver went into the waistcoat. When the coppers go out, nothing changes. He doesn't watch the drover leave. He rubs his thumbnail along something in his folded hand, small and pale, maybe a tally stick. Then he looks at Dov the way a man looks at someone who owes him and won't pay.

The drover pushes back through the crowd, grinning, his fist closed around the coins. He passes right over the cat.

The bond answers almost at once:

*On him now. In his hand, the coins. Same smell. Wet stone, candles. Weaker than the barrel, but the same.*

A moment later, more uneasy:

*Not the silver. Only the little ones.*

The drover gets six or seven steps up the bridge. Then his boot heel catches in a gap between the planks and he goes down hard on one knee. A copper jumps out of his fist and rolls. He swears, laughs, finds it against a post and pockets it. He limps on toward the north end, rubbing his knee, still pleased with himself.

At the barrel Dov is already calling again. *Find the lady, friends.* Between the stalls, the hooded man shifts his weight and goes back to counting silver.

The cat stays sitting among the boots, tail wrapped round its paws, waiting to hear what James wants next.

James and the cat catch up with the drover about forty feet up the bridge, where a chandler's lamp throws a yellow circle over the planks. The drover is limping, but not badly. Every few steps he stops to rub his knee and swear at the boards without much heat.

He looks round at the greeting. It's a broad, red face, with the cheerful wariness of a man who has just won money and knows what cities are like.

"Knee's had worse. Cow stood on it in Beregost once." He takes in the cloak, the rapier, the cat at James's boot. "Tobin Rusk. Drove forty head up the Way and sold 'em this morning, so if you're selling something, I've already been sold to." He grins at his own joke.

At *have a look at one* the grin narrows a little, and his fist stays shut.

"Odd how? Sharp's bloke, are you? Come to tell me it's a dud so you can swap it for a good one?" He looks at James a moment longer, then at the cat, which has sat down on the planks and is staring at his hand. Something about that seems to settle it. "Ah, go on. You look, I hold."

He opens his fist under the lamp. Eleven coppers and his own silver piece sit on a palm as hard as a saddle. The coppers are ordinary city pennies, worn smooth, a couple of them green at the rim. Tobin picks one up between finger and thumb and turns it edge-on to the light, as if to say *there, nothing up my sleeve*.

On the thin rim, where a penny has no business carrying anything, a mark has been pressed into the metal. It's tiny, no bigger than a grain of barley, and black, as though the copper had been burned there and not stamped. It's a branching shape: a single antler, the tines curving up.

Tobin tips another one. It carries the same mark, in the same place on the rim.

"Huh," he says. "Never noticed that." He closes his thumb over the coin a moment and laughs. "Warm, too. Well, it's been in my fist the whole way." He doesn't sound quite sure.

The bond stirs at James's feet, low and flat:

*Close now. Same smell. Stronger in his hand than on the bridge. The silver: nothing.*

The cat doesn't move any nearer.

Tobin holds his palm out a moment longer, then looks up at James with his fist half closed.

"So what is it, then? Somebody's mark? Am I going to have the Fist on me for spending it?"

James has seen this sign before, and not in a dealer's hand. He saw it in the margins of the first prayers he ever learned to the Lady, the ones a Tymoran learns so he knows what to keep from his door. It's the antler of Beshaba, the Maid of Misfortune, Lady Doom, Tymora's black sister. Her full sign is black antlers on a red field. Gamblers in the south spit when they see it scratched on a table. Sailors scrape it off a hull before they'll board. Down here on a penny it's only the one tine-branch, but it's the same shape. Nobody carves that mark by chance, and nobody puts it on something they mean to keep.

How it got into the copper, he can't tell. It isn't a die-stamp; the metal around it isn't pressed down. It isn't scratched either. It looks as though the copper was held against something hot no bigger than the mark, and the heat never quite left. Plain craft doesn't do that, but neither does any spell he knows. He looks at it until the lamp makes his eyes water and gets no further.

Tobin ties the sacking off with a twist of string and pushes the bundle deep into a different pocket from his silver. He pats it as if it might crawl out.

"You've gone a funny colour, friend." He tries a grin and doesn't quite manage it. "Go on, then. Whose is it?"

Tobin's face changes when he hears the name. It isn't fear exactly. It's what a country man looks like when a word his grandmother wouldn't say indoors is spoken out loud. He spits sideways onto the planks, quick and neat, and then looks a bit sheepish about it.

"My gran said you don't name her under a roof." He glances up at the eaves of the chandler's shop hanging over them. "Bridge is half a roof. Reckon that's half bad." The joke is thin, and he knows it.

At *I serve Tymora* he looks at the worn coin at James's neck, then at James's face, and something in his shoulders settles. He knows the type now: a man of the Lady. In Beregost they're the ones who pray over the dice before the harvest fair.

"Back to the Fist." He rubs his knee and doesn't look happy. "If she takes my money for evidence or some such, I'm walking. I hold 'em. She looks. Same as you."

They go back down the forty feet of bridge together, the cat a little ahead, its tail low. The queue has moved on by three carts. Sergeant Marrow is halfway through arguing with a carter over a lame mule when she sees them coming. She takes in James first, then the drover, then the sacking bundle in the drover's fist. Her mouth goes flat.

Tobin doesn't untie the bundle. He works one copper out through a gap in the sacking and holds it edge-on over the trestle, under her lamp, just as he did for James.

Marrow leans in. She doesn't touch it. She looks at the rim a long moment. The chalk in her fingers has stopped moving.

"Won it there?" She doesn't nod toward the barrel. She doesn't have to.

"Eleven of 'em," Tobin says. "And I near broke my knee after."

She opens the ledger. *RUSK* goes in under the evening's names in the same square hand. Her chalk hovers beside it, over the margin where the little crosses sit further up the column, and then she lifts it away without marking anything.

Behind James, thirty feet off, the cards are still slapping on the barrel. Then they stop for a beat. It's only half a breath, not long enough for the drovers to notice. Dov Penhallow's patter picks up again, *find the lady, friends*, a shade too bright.

"Put that away. Not here." Marrow says it to Tobin, but her eyes are on James. She keeps her voice down. "My relief's at the ninth bell. There's a pie-shop under Wyrm's Rock, the one with the blue shutter." She shuts the ledger. "The Lower City gate shuts not long after. Your bed, your choice."

She turns back to the carter and the lame mule as if they'd never come over.

Tobin pushes the copper back into the sacking and ties the bundle twice. He looks up the bridge toward the far walls, where the lamps of the Lower City are coming on, and then back at James.

"This priest of yours," he says. "Tonight? Because I was planning on being drunk tonight, and I'd like to know which way to point myself."

James sets off up the bridge with Tobin limping beside him. Wyrm's Crossing doesn't let anyone walk it fast. The houses lean in over the boards from both sides, and their upper floors nearly meet overhead, so the evening sky shows only as a thin strip between the eaves. Below, through gaps in the planking, the Chionthar shows black and moving. A man is frying onions on a brazier outside his own front door. Two children are dragging a crate of empty bottles that clink at every gap in the planks. A Fist patrol of three goes past the other way with their gauntlets hooked on their belts. They're talking about someone's sister and don't look at anybody.

The cat drops back. It doesn't follow at heel. It takes the shop thresholds, the dark under a cart, a windowsill, and keeps its head turned behind them.

The bond comes in pieces as they go:

*Barrel-man looked. Long, at your back. Then his hands again. He stays.*

A little later:

*Hood-man has not moved. Still counting. Nobody walks behind us. A dog, once. It went the other way.*

About halfway to the Rock, Tobin's left boot suddenly goes loose. The lace has snapped clean at the top eyelet. He catches himself on a post before the bad knee can take his weight again, and stands there holding the two ends.

"New laces," he says. "Bought 'em in Beregost a tenday back." He looks at the ends and doesn't laugh this time. He knots them together without saying anything, tight, and his hand goes once to the pocket with the sacking bundle before he walks on.

Wyrm's Rock rises out of the middle of the river, a squat old fortress of dark stone on its own island. The bridge splits to pass it, so the road runs along under its walls. Torches burn in brackets high up on the stone. Below them, wedged between the fortress footing and the first house of the north span, is a narrow shopfront with one shutter propped open on a stick. The shutter is painted blue, and the paint has faded to the colour of a winter sky. The smell of hot lard and pepper reaches them twenty feet off.

Inside there's one room, low and warm, with three tables and a bench along the wall. A big woman with flour up to her elbows is lifting a tray out of an oven built into the Rock's own stone. Behind her, painted straight onto the wall, is a menu that has been corrected so many times the old prices show through like ghosts. Two boatmen sit at the far table, eating and not talking. Nobody looks twice at the cat.

"Mutton, eel, or onion and cheese," the woman says without turning round. "Four copper a pie. Small beer's three a jug, ale's five. If you want the ale, you'd better want it hot, because the cask's next to the oven and there's nothing I can do about that."

Tobin lowers himself onto the bench with a grunt and puts his bad leg out straight. His eyes go to the ale on the wall.

"Mutton," he says to James, half a question. "If you're still buying."

He's watching the door, not the menu. Up the road the Rock's bell is quiet. The ninth bell is better than an hour off, and the pie-woman is waiting for an order.

The pie-woman doesn't turn round until she hears the coins on the board. Then she does, wipes her hands down her apron, and counts the eleven coppers with one floury finger. They go into a clay pot on the shelf. Two mutton pies come off the tray onto a board, each one split along the top and steaming, with a brown crust shiny with lard. A jug of small beer and two horn cups follow.

"Mind the gravy. It's hotter than it looks."

At *a shrine of Tymora* she gives James a short look, takes in the coin at his neck, and nods as if she'd half expected it.

"The Lady's Hall is up in the Upper City. That gate shut at dusk, and they don't open it for pie-folk, or for you." She jerks her chin north, through the wall of the Rock as though she could see past it. "There's the Lady's box, on a post by the Lower City gate. People drop a copper in for luck before they go under the arch. A young priestess comes down from the Hall some mornings and empties it. Red hair, very serious. She's been asking the gate-boys whether folk have stopped putting in." She shrugs. "I wouldn't know. I don't go in."

She turns back to the oven, then adds over her shoulder, "If you want a priest tonight, there's Twin Songs, out past the east side of the Outer City. They've a priest for every god there, and two for some. It's a long walk in the dark, though, and not one I'd make with a bad knee."

Tobin has already got his pie in both hands, burned his fingers on it and isn't letting go. He blows across the split crust, takes a bite that's far too big, and sits there breathing round it with his eyes watering.

"Tha's good," he says once he can, and swallows. "That's better than the Friendly Arm, and they charge you six for a pie that's mostly hope." He pours the small beer into both cups and slides one toward James, a shade carefully, watching the jug the whole way as if it might jump. Nothing spills. He looks faintly surprised.

"Morning, then, for your priestess." He says it to the pie, not to James. "Or a long walk. Or the sergeant first, and see what she's got." He glances at the door again, at the blue shutter on its stick and the dark road under the Rock. "I'll not lie, I'd sooner sit somewhere warm with this lot in my pocket than walk across half the Outer City with it."

Under the bench, the cat has curled itself round James's boot, where the oven's heat comes off the stone. Its ears are still turned toward Tobin's coat pocket.

*Warm here,* it says through the bond. *The smell is still there. It hasn't got worse.*

The two boatmen at the far table scrape back their stools, leave their coppers, and go out without a word. Up on the Rock the bell stays quiet. The ninth bell is still more than an hour off, so the evening can sit where it is until you decide to move it.

The pie-woman takes her time turning round. She wipes her hands, looks at the full board, the untouched pie, the cat under the bench, and seems to weigh it all.

"Keep it while you're eating. Once you stop eating, you're renting the bench." She jerks her chin at James's pie. "You've got a while on that one yet."

At Sergeant Marrow's name, one eyebrow goes up, and that's all the surprise she shows.

"Ilse comes in most nights after her relief. Eel, if there's any left." She lifts the lid on a covered tray, looks in and puts it back. "There'll be one. I keep it back."

For the room she points with a floury thumb, back toward the north span. "Mother Gannet. Three doors up past the Rock, over the rope-maker's, green door with a bell on a string. She boils her sheets, which is more than anyone else on this bridge does. It's five silver the night and another for a fire. She shuts the door at the last bell same as the gate does, so don't come knocking after."

Tobin has got through half his pie by now and slowed down to the pace of a man who intends to finish it. "Five silver for a bed over a river." He shakes his head at his cup. "In Beregost that buys you the bed and the farmer's daughter's opinion of you." He doesn't grin this time. He drinks.

James's pie sits on the board, steaming less now. The crust has stopped hissing.

When he gets to Pim, the boy looks up from the empty board. He scowls at being talked about, but he doesn't argue with any of it. Under the table his forearm stays across the tin. Wren has stopped moving at all.

"Losing on purpose isn't a crime." Marrow says it flatly, the way you put down a card you don't like. "Paying out of the wrong pocket isn't either. He pays his pitch. If I take him off the bridge for that, the captain asks why. Then I tell him about pennies, and he tells me about Umberlee." She turns the ledger a little on the board so it lines up with the table's edge. "So I need more than that."

She looks at the boy's tin, then at Tobin's coat.

"Benno had a copper in his teeth. I saw it when they laid him on the pier. I didn't look at the rim." She stops, then goes on. "I didn't know to. The captain had it thrown back in the river. Said that was proper."

She puts her finger on the open page again without looking at it.

"Here's what I've got that the captain hasn't bothered with. All seven came in from the south, on foot. Five from Elturel. Alone, or the next thing to it. Nobody with a cart, nobody with kin in the city to come asking." She turns back three leaves and taps a name, then another. "And none of them went into the water in the first tenday. They played a month. Two months. Then they went in."

Tobin has gone quiet on the bench. He's counting something on his fingers under the table and doesn't seem to know he's doing it.

"Lane behind the net sheds." Marrow's mouth tightens a little. "Moneylenders, pawn counters, a man who buys hair. Rivington's not my span. It's Corporal Dace's, and Dace's men don't walk that lane after dark unless they're paid to." She doesn't say who would pay them.

Then she turns to the Lady's Hall.

"Tonight, no. The Upper City gate's the Watch's. They don't open it for a Fist sergeant with a note about pennies, and they'd laugh at me in the morning for asking." She picks up the fork again. "Your red-haired girl comes down to the box at the north arch. Not every morning. The arch post is gate company, not mine, but the corporal there owes me a mule. I can leave a word that a man of the Lady wants her, and where to find him. That's the best I've got before the bells."

Tobin reaches for the jug to pour himself the last of the small beer, mostly to give his hands something to do. The handle comes away from the jug clean, with a dry little crack, and stays in his fist. The jug drops onto the board, rolls once, and goes over the edge. It breaks on the flags. Small beer runs out under the bench toward the cat, which gets up and moves without hurrying.

Tobin looks at the handle in his hand.

"That's three," he says quietly, and doesn't try to make it funny.

The pie-woman looks over her shoulder at the mess and says nothing. She takes a rag off the oven rail and throws it to him underhand. He catches it.

Marrow watched the whole thing. She looks at the jug's handle a while longer than she needs to, then at James.

"Safe." She wipes her thumb on her sleeve, though there's no chalk on it tonight. "The Rock's a Fist house. If I put the boy in it with a tin he won't give up, half the guardroom knows by morning, and the captain asks me why there's a fish-gutter on my bench." She glances at Pim, who has gone stiff at *Fist house*. "And he wouldn't stay. So, not the Rock."

"Gannet's is three doors up and she bolts at the last bell. Nobody gets past her bolt. My night man walks this end of the span on the hour. I can tell him to walk past her door."

Wren speaks before anyone else can, low and quick.

"We've our own place." She swallows. "We can't pay Mother Gannet. I won't have—" She stops and starts again, quieter. "The boathouse is ours."

"Benno's curtain's next to yours," Marrow says. She isn't unkind about it. It's just a fact, set down on the board like the ledger.

Wren doesn't answer that. She looks at James.

Pim says nothing. He's looking at the broken jug on the floor, and his arm is tight across the lid of the tin.

Up on the Rock the bell is quiet. The last bell, when both Gannet's door and the Lower City gate shut, is still a while off. Marrow has stopped talking. She's waiting to hear where the man of the Lady wants these three to sleep.

Three doors up the north span the rope-maker's shop is shuttered for the night, and coils of tarred line hang under the eaves like sleeping bats. James pulls the string. Somewhere inside a small brass bell rings. Bare feet cross a floor, and a hatch the size of a book opens at eye level.

Behind it is a sharp old face in a linen cap tied under the chin. She gives each of them a single look: the cloak and the rapier, the drover with the limp, the kindling girl, the boy with blood dried in his hair, and last of all the cat sitting on the top step.

"Wren," she says, surprised but not unfriendly. Then, to James, because he's the one who rang: "Mother Gannet. You'll be wanting beds, and you'll want them before the bell, same as everybody who comes up my stair at this hour."

The bolt draws back. Inside is a narrow hall that smells sharply of lye and lavender. The floorboards are scrubbed pale and there's a row of boots by the wall.

*Clean,* the cat says through the bond as it crosses the threshold, and sneezes. *Soap. Everything soap.* A pause. *The boy's tin is louder in here. Nothing else to hide behind.*

Mother Gannet holds up a candle and counts off on her fingers.

"Two rooms free. The back one's over the water, two beds and a truckle that pulls out, which'll do for a small one." She glances at Pim. "The front one's a bed and a chair, over the street, noisier. Five silver a room, a silver more for a fire in either. Boots off in the hall. And that boy washes his head in the basin before he goes near my sheets, or he sleeps on the boards."

Pim opens his mouth. Wren puts a hand on his shoulder and he shuts it again.

Mother Gannet waits with the candle, looking at James to see which rooms he wants and how many fires.

*Tin bowl now. Good. The boy's smell goes in there with him.*

"Boots off, all of you. The basin's in the kitchen and the boy goes first." She holds the light toward the narrow stair at the end of the hall. "Front room's at the top on the left. The back's straight on, over the water."

James sets his boots in the row by the wall, beside a pair of fishwife's clogs and somebody's good Sunday shoes. Tobin is still fighting his second boot. He has his bad leg straight out and is trying to reach it without bending the knee. James crouches, gets a hand under the heel and works it off in one long pull.

"Like pulling a calf the wrong way round," Tobin says, grinning at the ceiling. "Only the calf's grateful after." He wiggles his toes in a sock darned so often it's more darn than sock.

Mother Gannet takes Pim into the kitchen. James waits in the hall and hears most of it through the open door. There's water poured from a height. "Head down." A pause. "Lower." Pim says something sullen that gets lost in the splashing. Through the doorway James can see the boy bent over the basin with the tea-tin on the floor between his bare feet, pinned there by both ankles, while Mother Gannet scrubs the dried blood out of his hair with a rag and none of the patience she'd give a sheet. Wren stands just inside the door with a clean cloth over her arm. She doesn't help, because nobody asked her to.

Pim comes out with his hair wet and dark and sticking up. The pink line above his ear shows plainly now that the blood is gone. He has the tin under his arm again before he's finished drying his face.

"Clean," Mother Gannet says, as if she were signing for a delivery, and picks up her candle.

The stair is narrow and steep and it doesn't creak. At the top a small landing has two doors. The left one is open on the front room: one bed under a sloped ceiling, a rush-seated chair, a shuttered window onto the street. In the little grate, kindling that is definitely not Wren's has just caught under a split log, and it throws a moving orange light over everything. The dented pewter basin and the tin cup sit on the windowsill. Nothing in the room would break if you dropped it.

When James asks about the tin, Pim stops dead in the doorway.

He looks at the door, then at the tin, and then he looks at Wren.

"He wants it by the door." His tone makes it sound like a ridiculous idea. "By the door's where people *come in*."

"Pim."

"I'm only saying." He scowls round the room as if it had set him a trick question. Then he crosses to the chair, drags it over the boards to the foot of the bed and turns it so the seat faces the pillow. He puts the tin down on the rush seat, carefully, the way you'd put down an egg, and takes his hands off it. It's about six feet from where his head will be, and nowhere near the door.

"There." He's still talking to Wren. "In my sight. It's not in the bed. That's distance." He sits down on the edge of the mattress with his eyes on the painted lid, as though it might walk off.

Wren looks at the chair, then at James. She doesn't say it's what he asked for. She doesn't say it isn't, either.

Down at James's feet the cat has stopped on the threshold. It doesn't go in.

*Less on him now. A little,* the bond says. *The room has it. The chair has it. The boy still smells of it, like smoke after the fire's out.*

When James points across the landing to the other door, Pim's eyes go there for half a breath, then come back to the tin. He doesn't answer. He doesn't argue, either.

Wren answers for them both. She's standing in the doorway with the clean cloth still over her arm.

"We'll call." She swallows. "If anything breaks." She takes one end of her shawl in her hand and lets it go again. "Goodnight, Mister Worgen."

She shuts the door gently. Through it James hears the chair scrape an inch, Pim's voice low and cross, and then Wren's, lower.

The back room is straight on, over the water, as Mother Gannet said. It has two beds along the walls, a truckle pushed underneath one of them, and a window shuttered against the river. There's no fire, and the boards are cool under James's stocking feet. Under the floor the Chionthar works quietly at the piles. Tobin limps in behind him, looks at the nearer bed, then at the floor, and stamps once on the boards with his good foot to test them. They hold.

"Well," he says. "That's something."

Down in the hall Mother Gannet's candle goes along to the front door. The bolt hasn't gone across yet. The last bell is still a little way off. After that nobody comes up her stair, and nobody goes down it either. Nothing else is waiting on James before then unless he wants it to.

messages.text:
I turn away from the slap of cards before I can start following the lady.

Through our bond, I ask the cat, *What have you spotted?* I glance toward the gap between the shuttered stalls, keeping my place in line and my own senses.

When the sergeant calls me forward, I answer, “James Worgen. Former soldier, looking for honest work and a bed. Preferably the bed first.”

I count two copper into her palm. “Tethyr. Infantry, then scouts.”

Lowering my voice beneath the crowd’s noise, I add, “That fellow between the shuttered stalls is counting every silver at the card barrel. Could be nothing, but is that game usually here?”

I clear the checkpoint and stop at the riverside railing, out of the queue.

*Stay clear of the barrel,* I tell the cat through our bond. *Can you tell whether that smell clings to the coins people win, too? Don't touch them.*

While it noses about, I watch the next payout from a distance—particularly what the hooded watcher does when someone walks away with winnings.

*Come along,* I tell the cat, and walk after the limping drover.

“Bad turn on those planks. How’s the knee?” I fall into step beside him. “James Worgen. I saw you win back there—mind if I have a look at one of those copper winnings? Keep it in your palm. There’s something odd about them, and I’d rather you knew before spending them.”

“Not calling you a counterfeiter, Tobin. But the dealer paid those from a separate purse, and my cat won’t go near them. I’d keep them apart from your other money for now.”

Without touching the coins, I study the branching mark under the lamp, searching my knowledge of religion and magic for its meaning.
[Roll the die]
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

“Beshaba. Lady Misfortune.” I keep my voice low. “That’s her antler. I can’t tell you what’s been done to the coins, but I wouldn’t spend them—or pass them to someone else.”

I touch the worn coin at my neck. “I serve Tymora. This is rather pointedly my business.”

“Will you come back to Sergeant Marrow with me? She ought to see what’s being paid out on her bridge. After that, we can find a priest who knows how to deal with these safely.”

“Tonight, if we can find one. I don’t know the local clergy yet,” I admit. “But I’m not leaving you to carry that bundle alone. Let’s find the blue-shuttered pie-shop. Supper’s on me; I’ve delayed your drinking.”

I lead the way toward Wyrm’s Rock, keeping Tobin beside me.

Through the bond, I tell the cat, *Keep an eye behind us as we go. Tell me if the hooded man or the dealer follows—don’t confront either.*

“Two mutton pies and a jug of small beer, please.” I count out eleven copper from my own purse. “And do you know a shrine of Tymora nearby, or a priest staying on the bridge? We could use some advice tonight.”

I take the seat beside Tobin, leaving his stretched-out leg clear. “Still buying. Let’s get something in you besides worry.”

“Sergeant first,” I agree. “No dark roads on that knee if we can help it. If we must wait till morning, I’ll pay for a room here on the bridge.”

I let my pie cool before attempting what Tobin just survived.

To the pie-woman I say, “We’re waiting for Sergeant Marrow’s relief. May we keep the table until then? And who nearby lets a clean room?”

I put down my cup and turn toward her. “James. Come sit, Wren.”

I keep my voice low. “Your brother—has he been winning from the man with the card barrel? And has anything been going wrong for him afterward?”

I leave room for her to answer, then ask, “Where is he now?”

“Yes. You don’t owe me money, Wren. I’ll help him. I can’t promise I know how to break this yet, but I believe you.”

I turn to Tobin. “Will you stay here for Marrow? Tell her about Pim and Benno, and where we’ve gone. Keep those pennies wrapped.”

Then I look back to Wren. “Take me to your brother.”

I stop inside the curtain, keeping my hands away from my weapons.

“I’m James. Not Fist, and I’m not here to take your money.” I lower myself into a crouch so I’m not looming over him. “I used to play cards myself. I know how hard it is to let go of a winning purse.”

I glance at his bandage, then back to his face. “Another man won pennies tonight. They had a little black antler burned into the edge. Have yours got that mark too? You can hold the tin—I only want to look.”

“Because Dov lied to you.” I say it gently. “You picked the winning card, but those pennies carry Beshaba’s mark—the Lady of Misfortune. Not Tymora’s. I recognise it from my prayers.”

I leave my hands where he can see them. “I played cards for years, Pim. Won fortunes, lost them. Wanting the next win doesn’t make you stupid. But a dealer telling you never to spend your winnings ought to explain himself.”

“I don’t yet know how to make those coins safe. Will you leave the tin shut and come with Wren and me to the pie-shop? There’s a sergeant meeting us who’s seen the same pennies. You can tell her what Dov said yourself. You don’t have to face him.”

“Shut, and you carry it. Agreed. But if something starts going wrong, stop and tell me. Don’t try to brave it out.”

I stand carefully beneath the low eaves. “One thing before we go: where in Rivington have you seen Dov going with that purse?”

Once he’s answered, I lead them back toward the pie-shop, taking the damp stairs slowly and keeping close enough to help Pim if he stumbles.
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I pull out places for Wren and Pim, away from the oven. “A stair gave way under him. We caught him, but these pennies aren’t waiting politely for morning.”

I slide my untouched pie toward Pim. “Yours if you’re hungry. No bargain attached.”

Then I sit beside him. “That cut on your head—may I help it? Tymora’s given me a little healing. You needn’t hand over the tin.”

If he agrees, I spend one die of Healing Light on him.

I settle back beside the children. “We’ll stay here until Marrow arrives. No one needs to walk anywhere alone tonight.”

I keep watch over the table while Pim eats, waiting for the ninth bell and the sergeant’s arrival.

I touch the worn coin at my neck. “Tymora answered a prayer of mine. Her terms were that I give up cards and come to Baldur’s Gate. No instructions beyond that. I recognised her sister’s mark because her faithful are taught to.”

“Wren asked for help. That’s enough, orders or not.”

I keep my voice low. “I watched Dov deliberately let Tobin win. He took the stake into his waistcoat, but paid the marked coppers from a separate purse. Pim says Dov tells him to keep every penny, never spend them. Since then he’s suffered accidents—including a stair collapsing under him tonight.”

“Pim also saw Dov go toward the shops behind Rivington’s net sheds. Says Dov’s purse goes over flat on Firstday mornings and comes back full.”

I glance at the children, then back to Marrow. “First we need somewhere safe for these three, and a priest who can deal with those coins. Can you get word to the Lady’s Hall tonight?”

“Gannet’s. I’ll pay.” I turn to Wren. “One night, while we find help. It doesn’t mean giving up your home, and you owe me nothing.”

To Marrow: “Please leave word at the arch that James Worgen is at Mother Gannet’s with Beshaba-marked coins and people suffering repeated misfortune. Ask the priestess to come before emptying the Lady’s box—if anyone’s put a winning penny in there, she should know what to look for.”

I rise. “Thank you, Sergeant. We’ll tell you what we learn.”

Before we leave, I ask the pie-woman what I owe for the broken jug, and pay it from my own purse. Then I take the others to Gannet’s to arrange rooms before her door shuts.

“Both rooms, please. A fire in the front room only.” I count out eleven silver. “Wren and Pim can take the front bed. Tobin and I will take the back.”

Before she leads us up, I lower my voice. “There’s something you should know: we’ve reason to believe coins paid out at the bridge games are bringing misfortune on these two. Things have broken around them. We’re seeking a priest’s help, and Sergeant Marrow knows we’re here. I won’t hide that from you.”

I leave the silver where she can see it and wait for her answer before settling anyone in.

“Fair terms. Thank you.”

I take off my boots and help Tobin with his, then wait while Pim washes before we go upstairs.

At the front room, I ask Pim, “Would you put the closed tin beside the door tonight, rather than in bed with you? Still in your sight, still yours. Just give yourself a little distance from it.”

I point across the landing. “I’ll be right there. If anything breaks, or you need me for any reason, call. You won’t be bothering me.”

The strongest part was how personal the opening became without handing James a quest. The card game tempted him, the cat noticed something wrong, and his decision to investigate led naturally to Wren and Pim. Tymora mattered through his choices rather than through a divine instruction.

**What worked**
- The NPCs felt distinct and grounded. Marrow’s guarded concern, Tobin’s fading jokes, Gannet’s practical kindness, and Pim speaking through his sister all landed.
- Small accidents made the threat unsettling before it became overtly dangerous. Catching Pim on the stairs was the session’s best action moment.
- James could earn trust through concrete acts: supper, healing, lodging, and respecting Pim’s ownership of the tin. Those choices mattered without requiring constant Persuasion rolls.
- Failed Arcana left useful uncertainty instead of stopping the investigation.

**What broke or dragged**
- The pacing became very granular. Cooling a pie, ordering food, arranging beds, washing, and placing the tin each received substantial narration. Individually charming; cumulatively, they crowded out investigation.
- Several turns ended by reiterating that the bell had not rung and everyone was waiting. When I explicitly waited for Marrow, advancing straight to her arrival would have kept momentum.
- The unsolicited out-of-game explanations about the pie and which actions had already happened were distracting. Nothing needed defending or adjudicating there.
- Revealing Dov’s full name before James had learned it was a small viewpoint slip.

**What was missing**
- Clearer distances and remaining time before closing would help me make informed travel decisions.
- I wanted a little more room to test ideas about the coins. The investigation was compelling, but mostly advanced through NPC disclosures while my immediate role became caring for the victims.
- Resource tracking was generally clear, though the initial money conversion and rules discrepancies between the campaign sheet and opening records deserved a brief clarification.

Overall, I cared about these people and wanted to return. Keep the character detail and consequences; compress routine transitions so there’s more room for consequential choices in each session.

Yes—when the cat identified the marked winnings and I saw the hooded watcher counting stakes. I wanted to approach him separately and find out whether he was collecting for the Guild, watching Dov, or involved in the coins.

I didn’t because following Tobin seemed more urgent. Once Wren arrived, protecting Pim took priority, and I never returned to that lead. That felt like a genuine choice, not something the game prevented.

Later, I wanted to test whether putting the coins farther from their owners changed the misfortune. I only got as far as persuading Pim to put the tin outside his bed. I was reluctant to experiment around an injured child without knowing what might happen. A safer opportunity to investigate that would have been welcome.

James turns his shoulder to the barrel. The cards keep slapping behind him, *find the lady, friends*, and he stops listening.

The cat answers through the bond the way it always does, in pieces rather than words:

*A man. In the dark between the shut stalls. Still. Watching the barrel-man's hands. Not you.*

Then, sharper, with the feeling of fur rising along a spine:

*The barrel smells wrong. The little coins. Wet stone. Old candles. I don't like it.*

James lets his eyes drift down the bridge, the way a bored man looks around in a queue. Between the two shuttered stalls the lamplight gives out, and a young man leans in the gap with his hood up and his arms folded. He isn't looking at the queue or the river. Every time silver crosses the barrel his lips move a little, like someone keeping count. Then he goes still again.

James and the cat catch up with the drover about forty feet up the bridge, where a chandler's lamp throws a yellow circle over the planks. The drover is limping, but not badly. Every few steps he stops to rub his knee and swear at the boards without much heat.

He looks round at the greeting. It's a broad, red face, with the cheerful wariness of a man who has just won money and knows what cities are like.

"Knee's had worse. Cow stood on it in Beregost once." He takes in the cloak, the rapier, the cat at James's boot. "Tobin Rusk. Drove forty head up the Way and sold 'em this morning, so if you're selling something, I've already been sold to." He grins at his own joke.

At *have a look at one* the grin narrows a little, and his fist stays shut.

"Odd how? Sharp's bloke, are you? Come to tell me it's a dud so you can swap it for a good one?" He looks at James a moment longer, then at the cat, which has sat down on the planks and is staring at his hand. Something about that seems to settle it. "Ah, go on. You look, I hold."

He opens his fist under the lamp. Eleven coppers and his own silver piece sit on a palm as hard as a saddle. The coppers are ordinary city pennies, worn smooth, a couple of them green at the rim. Tobin picks one up between finger and thumb and turns it edge-on to the light, as if to say *there, nothing up my sleeve*.

On the thin rim, where a penny has no business carrying anything, a mark has been pressed into the metal. It's tiny, no bigger than a grain of barley, and black, as though the copper had been burned there and not stamped. It's a branching shape: a single antler, the tines curving up.

Tobin tips another one. It carries the same mark, in the same place on the rim.

"Huh," he says. "Never noticed that." He closes his thumb over the coin a moment and laughs. "Warm, too. Well, it's been in my fist the whole way." He doesn't sound quite sure.

The bond stirs at James's feet, low and flat:

*Close now. Same smell. Stronger in his hand than on the bridge. The silver: nothing.*

The cat doesn't move any nearer.

Tobin holds his palm out a moment longer, then looks up at James with his fist half closed.

"So what is it, then? Somebody's mark? Am I going to have the Fist on me for spending it?"

Tobin's face changes when he hears the name. It isn't fear exactly. It's what a country man looks like when a word his grandmother wouldn't say indoors is spoken out loud. He spits sideways onto the planks, quick and neat, and then looks a bit sheepish about it.

"My gran said you don't name her under a roof." He glances up at the eaves of the chandler's shop hanging over them. "Bridge is half a roof. Reckon that's half bad." The joke is thin, and he knows it.

At *I serve Tymora* he looks at the worn coin at James's neck, then at James's face, and something in his shoulders settles. He knows the type now: a man of the Lady. In Beregost they're the ones who pray over the dice before the harvest fair.

"Back to the Fist." He rubs his knee and doesn't look happy. "If she takes my money for evidence or some such, I'm walking. I hold 'em. She looks. Same as you."

They go back down the forty feet of bridge together, the cat a little ahead, its tail low. The queue has moved on by three carts. Sergeant Marrow is halfway through arguing with a carter over a lame mule when she sees them coming. She takes in James first, then the drover, then the sacking bundle in the drover's fist. Her mouth goes flat.

Tobin doesn't untie the bundle. He works one copper out through a gap in the sacking and holds it edge-on over the trestle, under her lamp, just as he did for James.

Marrow leans in. She doesn't touch it. She looks at the rim a long moment. The chalk in her fingers has stopped moving.

turns.reply:
James sets off up the bridge with Tobin limping beside him. Wyrm's Crossing doesn't let anyone walk it fast. The houses lean in over the boards from both sides, and their upper floors nearly meet overhead, so the evening sky shows only as a thin strip between the eaves. Below, through gaps in the planking, the Chionthar shows black and moving. A man is frying onions on a brazier outside his own front door. Two children are dragging a crate of empty bottles that clink at every gap in the planks. A Fist patrol of three goes past the other way with their gauntlets hooked on their belts. They're talking about someone's sister and don't look at anybody.

The cat drops back. It doesn't follow at heel. It takes the shop thresholds, the dark under a cart, a windowsill, and keeps its head turned behind them.

The bond comes in pieces as they go:

*Barrel-man looked. Long, at your back. Then his hands again. He stays.*

A little later:

*Hood-man has not moved. Still counting. Nobody walks behind us. A dog, once. It went the other way.*

About halfway to the Rock, Tobin's left boot suddenly goes loose. The lace has snapped clean at the top eyelet. He catches himself on a post before the bad knee can take his weight again, and stands there holding the two ends.

"New laces," he says. "Bought 'em in Beregost a tenday back." He looks at the ends and doesn't laugh this time. He knots them together without saying anything, tight, and his hand goes once to the pocket with the sacking bundle before he walks on.

Wyrm's Rock rises out of the middle of the river, a squat old fortress of dark stone on its own island. The bridge splits to pass it, so the road runs along under its walls. Torches burn in brackets high up on the stone. Below them, wedged between the fortress footing and the first house of the north span, is a narrow shopfront with one shutter propped open on a stick. The shutter is painted blue, and the paint has faded to the colour of a winter sky. The smell of hot lard and pepper reaches them twenty feet off.

Inside there's one room, low and warm, with three tables and a bench along the wall. A big woman with flour up to her elbows is lifting a tray out of an oven built into the Rock's own stone. Behind her, painted straight onto the wall, is a menu that has been corrected so many times the old prices show through like ghosts. Two boatmen sit at the far table, eating and not talking. Nobody looks twice at the cat.

"Mutton, eel, or onion and cheese," the woman says without turning round. "Four copper a pie. Small beer's three a jug, ale's five. If you want the ale, you'd better want it hot, because the cask's next to the oven and there's nothing I can do about that."

Tobin lowers himself onto the bench with a grunt and puts his bad leg out straight. His eyes go to the ale on the wall.

"Mutton," he says to James, half a question. "If you're still buying."

He's watching the door, not the menu. Up the road the Rock's bell is quiet. The ninth bell is better than an hour off, and the pie-woman is waiting for an order.

They go into a clay pot on the shelf. Two mutton pies come off the tray onto a board, each one split along the top and steaming, with a brown crust shiny with lard. A jug of small beer and two horn cups follow.

"Mind the gravy. It's hotter than it looks."

At *a shrine of Tymora* she gives James a short look, takes in the coin at his neck, and nods as if she'd half expected it.

"The Lady's Hall is up in the Upper City. That gate shut at dusk, and they don't open it for pie-folk, or for you." She jerks her chin north, through the wall of the Rock as though she could see past it. "There's the Lady's box, on a post by the Lower City gate. People drop a copper in for luck before they go under the arch. A young priestess comes down from the Hall some mornings and empties it. Red hair, very serious. She's been asking the gate-boys whether folk have stopped putting in." She shrugs. "I wouldn't know. I don't go in."

She turns back to the oven, then adds over her shoulder, "If you want a priest tonight, there's Twin Songs, out past the east side of the Outer City. They've a priest for every god there, and two for some. It's a long walk in the dark, though, and not one I'd make with a bad knee."

Tobin has already got his pie in both hands, burned his fingers on it and isn't letting go. He blows across the split crust, takes a bite that's far too big, and sits there breathing round it with his eyes watering.

"Tha's good," he says once he can, and swallows. "That's better than the Friendly Arm, and they charge you six for a pie that's mostly hope." He pours the small beer into both cups and slides one toward James, a shade carefully, watching the jug the whole way as if it might jump. Nothing spills. He looks faintly surprised.

"Morning, then, for your priestess." He says it to the pie, not to James. "Or a long walk. Or the sergeant first, and see what she's got." He glances at the door again, at the blue shutter on its stick and the dark road under the Rock. "I'll not lie, I'd sooner sit somewhere warm with this lot in my pocket than walk across half the Outer City with it."

Under the bench, the cat has curled itself round James's boot, where the oven's heat comes off the stone. Its ears are still turned toward Tobin's coat pocket.

*Warm here,* it says through the bond. *The smell is still there. It hasn't got worse.*

The two boatmen at the far table scrape back their stools, leave their coppers, and go out without a word. Up on the Rock the bell stays quiet. The ninth bell is still more than an hour off, so the evening can sit where it is until you decide to move it.

James puts down his cup. Wren looks at the bench before she sits on it, as if she doesn't think it's meant for her. Then she perches on the very end, her back straight and her feet tucked under, and keeps the shawl ends wound tight in both hands. Tobin shifts his bad leg to give her room and says nothing. For once he isn't joking.

"Wren," she says, though James already has it from the pie-woman. "Thank you."

At his first question she nods before he's finished asking.

"The barrel, mostly. The man with the waistcoat." It comes out fast and low, like the speech she practised on the way. "Sometimes the cups man by the fish steps, but mostly the barrel. Since the thaw. He goes most evenings with whatever he's earned gutting. A silver if he has one. He comes home with pennies. Always pennies. Never loses." She stops. "Nobody never loses."

She swallows and goes on to what's been going wrong.

"It started small. He cut his hand on a gutting knife, and he's good with a knife. Our landlord's dog bit him, and it's an old dog, it doesn't bite anybody. Then the fishmonger let him go because the barrels kept tipping when he carried them." She looks down at her hands. "Last tenday a tile came off a roof on the Rivington side and opened his head here." She touches her own hairline, above the left ear. "And plates crack. I'm not telling stories. He walks past the shelf and one cracks right across. I've seen it twice."

Tobin's hand has gone to his coat pocket, the one with the sacking bundle. He holds it there, flat.

"He keeps the pennies in a tin under his pallet. He won't spend them. Says they're his lucky ones, because he won them. He won't let me touch the tin." Her voice catches on that, and she pushes through it. "There was a man in the next loft. Benno. He played the barrel too, all winter. The Fist pulled him out by the Rivington piers a tenday back, with a copper in his mouth. People say it's the sea taking her due." She shakes her head once. "Benno was frightened of the water. He never went near the edge."

When James asks where her brother is, she answers at once. This part she's sure of.

"Home. Hask's boathouse, under the south end of the bridge. Down the water stairs, the lofts over the boats. I made him promise to stay in tonight." A short pause. "Pim. His name's Pim. He's thirteen."

She looks at James then, straight at him, not at the cat or the coin at his neck.

"I can't pay you. Not in money. But I sell kindling up and down this bridge every day, both ends, and nobody looks at the kindling girl. I see who goes where." She takes a breath. "Somebody's doing this to them. You knew the penny was wrong, and you took it to the Fist instead of laughing. So I'm asking. Will you help Pim?"

She doesn't say anything else. Her hands stay knotted in the shawl, and she waits for him to say no.

James says yes, and Wren doesn't seem to take it in at first. She keeps looking at him, braced for something that doesn't come. Then she nods once, quickly, and gets up off the end of the bench.

"Thank you." She says nothing more. She's already turning toward the door.

Tobin looks at the bundle in his pocket, then at the oven, then at James. He lets out a long breath through his nose.

"Sit by a hot oven and wait for a woman to walk in. Best job anyone's given me all year." The joke comes out flat, and he doesn't try to grin. "Aye. I'll tell her. The boy, Pim. The other one, Benno, out of the water by Rivington. Hask's boathouse, down the water stairs." He puts his hand flat on the pocket. "And these stay tied. Go on."

The pie-woman says nothing. She glances at James's pie, still whole on its board, and then goes back to her oven.

Wren takes him south, back the way he came. She keeps to the edge of the planks next to the house-fronts and walks fast, a step ahead. The cat goes in front of them both, low, from doorstep to doorstep. A man is still frying onions outside his door. As they get near the south end the lamps get farther apart, and the noise of the checkpoint comes back: the chalk on the board, a carter swearing, Marrow's flat "Next."

Then they pass the barrel.

Dov Penhallow has four drovers and a tinker at his barrel. He's bent over the cards with a silver piece pinned under one finger, and he's laughing at something one of them said. He doesn't look up as they go by behind the crowd. In the dark gap between the shuttered stalls, the hooded young man is still counting.

At the trestle, Sergeant Marrow's eyes come up from the ledger. They go to James, then to the girl in the brown shawl beside him, and back down to the page. She doesn't stop writing.

The water stairs start just past the last house on the south span. They're a narrow wooden flight bolted to the side of the bridge pier, going down into the dark with a rope for a handrail. The treads are black and soft with river damp. Wren goes down them without looking, the way you take stairs you've used a thousand times. Halfway down the cat stops and looks back up at James, then carries on.

Hask's boathouse sits under the bridge, built between two of the great stone piers. It's one long shed on stilts over the water, and the Chionthar slaps at the pilings underneath. Below, the boats hang in rope slings, three hulls turned keel-up for caulking, and the air is thick with tar and wet wood. Above them, reached by ladders, a loft runs the whole length of the shed. It has been split up with hung sacking and old sailcloth into a dozen little rooms. Lamplight shows through the cloth in patches. Someone is singing to a baby in a tired voice. Someone else is cooking turnips. A man with a burned face sits on a crate at the foot of the nearest ladder mending a net. He looks at James's rapier, at Wren, and goes back to his knots without saying a word.

Wren goes up the third ladder. At the top she stops in front of one curtain and doesn't look at it. It's grey sailcloth, tied shut with string, and nothing moves behind it.

"Benno's," she says quietly, and pushes the next curtain aside.

The room is the width of two pallets. There's a shelf nailed to a post with a clay jug, two cups and a heel of bread on it. A lamp burns low on an upturned crate. On the pallet nearer the eaves, a boy sits with his back against the planks and his knees pulled up. He's thin like his sister, with the same chin. A rag is bound round his head above the left ear, and it has gone rust-brown in one spot. His fish-gutter's hands are scarred across the knuckles, and when the curtain moves they go straight down between the pallet and the wall.

The bond comes in sharp and close, and the cat's fur is standing up all along its back:

*Strong. Here, much stronger. Under the boy's bed. Wet stone, candles, so much of it. It's on him too, all over him, like smoke on clothes.*

"You said you were just going to the pie-shop." Pim talks to his sister, but he's staring at James: the cloak, the blade, the cat. "Who's he? You said you wouldn't bring the Fist."

"He's not Fist." Wren drops the curtain behind them. "He knows about the pennies, Pim."

The boy's hand closes on something under the pallet. Wood scrapes on wood, and the edge of a tin box shows: a dented old tea-tin with a painted lid worn down to bare metal.

On the shelf above his head, the clay jug cracks. It's a short, dry sound. A line runs from the lip to the base, and water starts to bead along it and run down onto the planks.

Nobody's touched it. Wren's face goes very still.

Pim doesn't look at the jug. He holds onto the tin with both hands.

"They're mine," he says. "I won them. Every one."

I stop inside the curtain, keeping my hands away from my weapons.

“I’m James. Not Fist, and I’m not here to take your money.” I lower myself into a crouch so I’m not looming over him. “I used to play cards myself. I know how hard it is to let go of a winning purse.”

I glance at his bandage, then back to his face. “Another man won pennies tonight. They had a little black antler burned into the edge. Have yours got that mark too? You can hold the tin—I only want to look.”
turns.reply:
James stays just inside the curtain with his hands loose and empty. Then he crouches, his cloak folding on the damp planks, until his head is lower than the boy's.

Pim watches him come down the way a dog watches a man pick up a stick. His hands stay on the tin.

At *I used to play cards myself* something flickers in his face. It isn't trust, but it's interest. He looks at Wren, not at James.

"He plays?" Then, a little louder, to the planks between them: "What'd you play?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. At the mention of the antler his eyes snap back to James's face, sharp and suspicious, the way a man looks when a stranger knows something he thought was his.

"Who's been showing you mine?"

"Nobody," Wren says quietly from the curtain. "It was a drover's. Tonight. Same barrel."

Pim chews on that. The water drips off the cracked jug onto the planks behind his head, slow and steady, and he doesn't turn round to it. At last he drags the tin out from between the pallet and the wall and sets it on his knees. He keeps both hands flat on the lid. Then he lifts one edge a finger's width, toward the lamp and away from James, the way a boy shows you a bird's egg without letting you near it.

Inside, the coppers lie loose and dull, a small heap of them, more than twenty and maybe thirty. They're worn city pennies like Tobin's. Pim tips the tin so one slides against the rim and turns it edge-up with his scarred thumb. The little black antler sits on the edge, tines curving up, burned into the metal.

"They've all got it." He says it proudly. "Every one. That's how you know they're won ones. Dov says." He lifts his chin. "Dov says keep 'em, don't spend 'em, 'cause a won penny's a lucky penny, and if you spend it the luck goes with it. And I *don't* lose. Not once since the thaw."

The bond comes up hard the moment the lid opens. Behind James, the cat has backed into the curtain until the sailcloth bulges round it.

*Open. It's coming out like steam. Wet stone. Candles. Cold-wet, on my nose. Close it.*

Pim lets the lid drop shut with a tinny click and puts both forearms across it. He looks at the rag on his own head, or tries to, with his eyes rolled up, and then he looks at James again. For the first time he looks a little less sure.

"So go on, then. You're the card man." His voice cracks a little on it, and he scowls to cover it. "If they're lucky, how come everything keeps breaking?"

“Because Dov lied to you.” I say it gently. “You picked the winning card, but those pennies carry Beshaba’s mark—the Lady of Misfortune. Not Tymora’s. I recognise it from my prayers.”

I leave my hands where he can see them. “I played cards for years, Pim. Won fortunes, lost them. Wanting the next win doesn’t make you stupid. But a dealer telling you never to spend your winnings ought to explain himself.”

“I don’t yet know how to make those coins safe. Will you leave the tin shut and come with Wren and me to the pie-shop? There’s a sergeant meeting us who’s seen the same pennies. You can tell her what Dov said yourself. You don’t have to face him.”
turns.reply:
Pim doesn't interrupt. When James says *Beshaba*, the boy's face goes blank. It isn't fear. He's never heard the name, and he doesn't like a stranger knowing a word he doesn't. Wren knows it, though. Over by the curtain her hands go still in her shawl.

"Dov don't explain nothing." He says it to the tin. "Says *well played, friend*, and that's it. He's not even crossing. He comes over from Rivington, Firstday mornings, early, when I'm on the fish. His little purse goes over flat and comes back fat." He scowls. "I thought he was winning it off somebody over there."

At the mention of a sergeant his head comes up sharply, and he looks at his sister, not at James.

"You said no Fist."

"I said he wasn't Fist," Wren says quietly. "He isn't. She's the one at the toll. Marrow. She doesn't shout."

Pim chews on that. Then he gets up off the pallet in one quick, ungainly move, the way thirteen-year-olds do everything, and nearly cracks his bandaged head on the eaves. He ducks just in time. He has the tin clamped under his arm and shut, with his whole forearm over the lid.

"I'll come." He's still talking to Wren. "But it comes with me. I'm not leaving it here with Benno's curtain next door and the whole loft knowing where I sleep. Somebody'd have it before the bell." He finally turns to James and lifts his chin. "Shut. Like you said. I won't open it. But it's mine and it stays on me."

Down by the curtain the cat has stopped backing away. It sits with its tail wrapped tight, looking at the boy's arm.

*Closed is better. Still on him. It goes where he goes.*

Wren takes her shawl ends in both hands and looks at James. She's waiting to see whether that's good enough.

“Shut, and you carry it. Agreed. But if something starts going wrong, stop and tell me. Don’t try to brave it out.”

I stand carefully beneath the low eaves. “One thing before we go: where in Rivington have you seen Dov going with that purse?”

Once he’s answered, I lead them back toward the pie-shop, taking the damp stairs slowly and keeping close enough to help Pim if he stumbles.
turns.reply:
James nods to the tin, and Pim's chin comes down a little.

"Fine," the boy says to Wren, as though she'd made the deal. Then, with a quick look at James: "I'm not braving nothing."

James straightens slowly under the low eaves, and Pim scowls at the question about Rivington. He doesn't like having been seen watching.

"Past the Rivington piers. Where they found Benno." He says it flat and fast. "There's a lane behind the net sheds, lots of little shops. Moneylenders, a cooper, a man who buys hair. I followed Dov once. I wanted to see who he was winning off." His mouth twists. "He went in one of the shops, and I didn't see which, 'cause a dog came out from under a cart and had me by the trousers. Tore 'em right up the back." He touches his hip, where the patch must be. "That was before the tile."

Wren looks at him. She hadn't heard about the dog.

They go out past Benno's tied curtain and down the ladder. The net-mender at the bottom doesn't look up. Out on the landing the river sounds louder in the dark, slapping at the piles under the shed. The water stairs climb the pier into the lamplight above, black and shining with damp.

Wren goes first because she knows the treads. Pim goes after her with the tin clamped under his left arm, which leaves only his right hand for the rope. James comes up right behind him, close enough to touch the boy's back. The cat follows James, one tread at a time, its ears flat.

*The tin is on the stairs now,* comes through the bond. *Wrong. Near the water it's wrong.*

About halfway up, a tread that has held a thousand times tilts under Pim's foot. The bolt at one end gives with a soft, rotten crunch, and the plank swings down like a trapdoor. His foot goes with it. His right hand jerks on the rope, and his left arm won't let go of the tin.

James is already moving when the plank drops. Years of scouting have taught his body that ground is never trustworthy. His left hand closes on the back of Pim's collar, his right gets a fistful of rope, and he plants his boot on the tread below as the boy's weight comes onto him. For a moment Pim hangs there with one leg kicking over open air and the black river under it, the tin still crushed against his ribs. Then James hauls him back up the stairs in one smooth pull. The boy's knees hit the next sound tread, and his arm never comes off the lid.

The broken plank swings once on its last bolt, tears loose and drops. It hits the water with a flat smack, and the Chionthar takes it under the boathouse without a ripple.

In the quiet afterwards, James feels the old coin against his breastbone grow warm. It isn't from his own skin. It feels like someone just pressed a thumb to it, the way a dealer touches a winning card.

Pim stays kneeling, breathing hard. He looks down at the gap where the tread was, then at James's hand still knotted in his collar. He doesn't say thank you. He says, too loudly, to Wren up above him:

"That stair's been fine since we came."

"I know," Wren says. Her hand is reaching back down toward him, and it isn't steady.

James keeps hold until the boy is on his feet. They take the rest of the stairs slowly, Pim testing every tread with his toe now, and come out onto the boards of the south span into lamplight and onion smoke.

The checkpoint is still working. Marrow's chalk taps, and a pedlar argues about the toll on a handcart. She doesn't look up this time, though James has the feeling she has counted all three of them.

The barrel comes next. Dov has only two drovers now, and he's shuffling slowly, lazily. As they pass behind the crowd his eyes come up from the cards and land on Pim, on the boy he knows from a whole winter of evenings, walking beside the man with the cat. His hands don't stop. The patter doesn't stop either. *Find the lady, friends.* But his gaze follows them a step longer than it would follow anybody else, and then it drops to the tin under Pim's arm.

Pim sees him looking. He lifts his chin and keeps walking.

*Barrel-man saw the boy,* the cat says. *Saw the tin. Then you.*

In the dark between the shuttered stalls, the hooded man is still counting silver.

The walk north under the leaning houses takes ten minutes or so. Nothing else breaks. Near the Rock, Pim swaps the tin to his other arm without loosening his grip and mutters, "Heavy," to nobody.

The blue shutter is still propped on its stick. Inside it's warm and smells of pepper. Tobin is on the bench with his bad leg out, a second jug of small beer in front of him that he's barely touched, and one hand flat on his coat pocket. He looks up when the stick creaks. His eyes go to the boy with the bloody rag round his head, then to the tin, and he breathes out through his nose.

"That's him, then." Then, to James: "She's not come. Not the ninth bell yet."

James's pie is still on its board where he left it, cold now. The pie-woman glances at the newcomers, at the tin, and says nothing.

The ninth bell is still a little way off, and Marrow is still at her trestle at the south end.

turns.reply:
James pulls the stool out from the end of the table, away from the heat of the oven, and drags a second one over from the empty table where the boatmen sat. Wren takes hers without a word. Pim looks at his for a moment, then sits on its very edge with the tin across his knees.

At *a stair gave way* Tobin's eyes go to the boy's legs and then to his own knee, which is still stretched out along the bench. He doesn't make a joke of it.

"Did it, now," he says quietly. "Well, there's a pair of us."

The pie-woman doesn't turn round. Her rolling pin stops for a moment, though, and then starts again.

James pushes the cold pie across the board. Pim stares at it. He looks at James, then at Wren, then back at the pie. He reads it like a deal he can't see the catch in.

"No bargain," he says to his sister, flatly, checking.

"He said," Wren answers.

The boy keeps one forearm across the tin and reaches with the other hand. He tears off half the crust in one go and eats it fast, hunched over, the way you eat in a loft where somebody else might want it. Gravy runs over his scarred knuckles and he licks it off without a pause. Wren watches him. Her hands have come loose from her shawl.

When James sits down beside him and asks about the cut, Pim stops chewing.

"Healing," he says through the pie. "Like a priest does." His eyes go to the coin on its cord at James's neck, then to the rag on his own head. Something in him wants to say no on principle, and something else is remembering the tile. "Does it hurt?"

"Pim," Wren says.

"I'm asking." He swallows. Then, to Wren rather than to James: "Fine. Head only. He doesn't touch the tin."

He leans his head a little toward James and keeps his arm tight across the lid.

James lays two fingers lightly against the stained rag above the boy's ear. The warmth gathers under his breastbone first, where the coin sits, and then runs down his arm like sunlight moving across a table.

For a breath a soft gold light shows through the rag, faint as a candle through a curtain. Pim flinches. It doesn't hurt. He just wasn't expecting to feel anything. Under James's fingers the skin pulls together, and when the light fades the boy puts his own hand up and works the rag loose. The dried blood is still crusted in his hair, but under it there's only a raw pink line where the tile opened him. The cut has closed.

Pim feels along it with his fingertips, once and then again. He doesn't say anything. He picks up the rest of the pie.

Wren lets out a breath she's clearly been holding since the stairs. "Thank you," she says, low, for both of them.

Under the table the cat has stayed curled round James's boot. Its ears haven't moved from the tin.

*His head is better. I smell less blood.* A pause, then flatter: *The other smell is the same. The light didn't touch it.*

Tobin has watched the whole thing over the rim of his cup. He sets it down carefully.

"Well, that's a thing to see in a pie-shop." He looks at his own knee, then thinks better of whatever he was going to ask and drinks instead.

Up on the Rock the bell is still quiet. The pie-woman slides the covered eel tray to the warm end of the oven, where she keeps the sergeant's supper.

I settle back beside the children. “We’ll stay here until Marrow arrives. No one needs to walk anywhere alone tonight.”

I keep watch over the table while Pim eats, waiting for the ninth bell and the sergeant’s arrival.
turns.reply:
James sits back down on the bench beside the children, with his back to the Rock's warm stone and the door where he can see it. Nobody argues. Wren unwinds her shawl a little in the heat. Tobin pulls his bad leg in so it won't be in the way.

Pim eats the rest of the pie slowly now, the way you eat when nobody's going to take it from you. He scrapes the gravy off the board with his thumb. Then he wipes the thumb on his trousers and sits looking at the empty board with the tin on his knees.

"How much," he says to Wren, as though James weren't sitting a foot away, "is a fortune, anyway? In silver."

"Pim."

"I'm only asking what it *is*." He doesn't look at James, but he waits.

The pie-woman lifts a fresh tray out of the oven. One of the boatmen's coppers is still lying on the far table, and she sweeps it into her apron pocket on the way past. Under the bench the cat has its chin on James's boot and its eyes half shut, but its ears haven't moved off Pim's knees. Out on the road a cart rattles by under the Rock, and then a pair of Fist boots goes past without slowing.

A little later the bell up on Wyrm's Rock begins: nine slow strokes, heavy enough that the cups hum faintly on the board. Tobin counts them under his breath and stops at five, like a man who's lost a head of cattle out of the count and given up.

A few minutes after the ninth stroke the shutter-stick creaks.

Sergeant Ilse Marrow ducks in under the blue shutter in her red coat with the gauntlet off. There's a flat bundle in oilcloth under her arm. She looks round the room once, the way she reads a queue: James, Tobin, the girl in the brown shawl, the boy with the bloody hair and the tin. Her face doesn't change.

"Hm."

The pie-woman has the eel pie on a board before Marrow reaches the table. Marrow puts four coppers down without being asked and the pie-woman takes them without a word. It's clearly an old arrangement. Marrow sits on the stool across from James, puts the bundle next to her pie, and doesn't touch either.

Tobin clears his throat. "I was meant to tell you, the boy and the drowned fellow, Benno, and the boathouse, only he's gone and brought them himself, so." He trails off. "So that's told."

"Benno Faell." Marrow says it to the oilcloth. "Out of the water by the Rivington piers, eleven days back. Copper in his teeth." She unties the bundle. It's the ledger from the trestle, a working book with the spine split and mended with thread. "Captain calls it Umberlee's tithe and says it's a matter for the priests of the sea. Umberlee's priestesses take what's thrown in. They don't come up the river looking for it."

She opens the book at a page near the front and turns it so it faces James. The page is from last autumn, in the same square capitals. There are columns of names, and dates, and *on foot*, *cart*, *with family*. A few lines down, a small chalk cross sits beside a name, gone soft and grey with handling.

"Seven since the leaves fell." Her finger stops on the last one. *FAELL, BENNO, on foot, from Elturel, alone.* There's a fresh-looking cross beside it. "All seven came through my table. Marrow picks up her fork at last and breaks the crust on the eel pie. Steam comes up. She doesn't eat yet.
