I touch the worn coin at my neck. “Tymora answered a prayer of mine. Her terms were that I give up cards and come to Baldur’s Gate. No instructions beyond that. I recognised her sister’s mark because her faithful are taught to.”

“Wren asked for help. That’s enough, orders or not.”

I keep my voice low. “I watched Dov deliberately let Tobin win. He took the stake into his waistcoat, but paid the marked coppers from a separate purse. Pim says Dov tells him to keep every penny, never spend them. Since then he’s suffered accidents—including a stair collapsing under him tonight.”

“Pim also saw Dov go toward the shops behind Rivington’s net sheds. Says Dov’s purse goes over flat on Firstday mornings and comes back full.”

I glance at the children, then back to Marrow. “First we need somewhere safe for these three, and a priest who can deal with those coins. Can you get word to the Lady’s Hall tonight?”
turns.reply:
James touches the worn coin at his neck. Marrow watches his hand go to it and then looks back at his face. She lets him finish without interrupting. Her fork stays in the crust of the eel pie.

At *give up cards* her eyes flick, just once, to the deck-shaped lump in the corner of his pack. She says nothing about it.

At *a separate purse* she sets the fork down.

When he gets to Pim, the boy looks up from the empty board. He scowls at being talked about, but he doesn't argue with any of it. Under the table his forearm stays across the tin. Wren has stopped moving at all.

"Losing on purpose isn't a crime." Marrow says it flatly, the way you put down a card you don't like. "Paying out of the wrong pocket isn't either. He pays his pitch. If I take him off the bridge for that, the captain asks why. Then I tell him about pennies, and he tells me about Umberlee." She turns the ledger a little on the board so it lines up with the table's edge. "So I need more than that."

She looks at the boy's tin, then at Tobin's coat.

"Benno had a copper in his teeth. I saw it when they laid him on the pier. I didn't look at the rim." She stops, then goes on. "I didn't know to. The captain had it thrown back in the river. Said that was proper."

She puts her finger on the open page again without looking at it.

"Here's what I've got that the captain hasn't bothered with. All seven came in from the south, on foot. Five from Elturel. Alone, or the next thing to it. Nobody with a cart, nobody with kin in the city to come asking." She turns back three leaves and taps a name, then another. "And none of them went into the water in the first tenday. They played a month. Two months. Then they went in."

Tobin has gone quiet on the bench. He's counting something on his fingers under the table and doesn't seem to know he's doing it.

"Lane behind the net sheds." Marrow's mouth tightens a little. "Moneylenders, pawn counters, a man who buys hair. Rivington's not my span. It's Corporal Dace's, and Dace's men don't walk that lane after dark unless they're paid to." She doesn't say who would pay them.

Then she turns to the Lady's Hall.

"Tonight, no. The Upper City gate's the Watch's. They don't open it for a Fist sergeant with a note about pennies, and they'd laugh at me in the morning for asking." She picks up the fork again. "Your red-haired girl comes down to the box at the north arch. Not every morning. The arch post is gate company, not mine, but the corporal there owes me a mule. I can leave a word that a man of the Lady wants her, and where to find him. That's the best I've got before the bells."

Tobin reaches for the jug to pour himself the last of the small beer, mostly to give his hands something to do. The handle comes away from the jug clean, with a dry little crack, and stays in his fist. The jug drops onto the board, rolls once, and goes over the edge. It breaks on the flags. Small beer runs out under the bench toward the cat, which gets up and moves without hurrying.

Tobin looks at the handle in his hand.

"That's three," he says quietly, and doesn't try to make it funny.

The pie-woman looks over her shoulder at the mess and says nothing. She takes a rag off the oven rail and throws it to him underhand. He catches it.

Marrow watched the whole thing. She looks at the jug's handle a while longer than she needs to, then at James.

"Safe." She wipes her thumb on her sleeve, though there's no chalk on it tonight. "The Rock's a Fist house. If I put the boy in it with a tin he won't give up, half the guardroom knows by morning, and the captain asks me why there's a fish-gutter on my bench." She glances at Pim, who has gone stiff at *Fist house*. "And he wouldn't stay. So, not the Rock."

"Gannet's is three doors up and she bolts at the last bell. Nobody gets past her bolt. My night man walks this end of the span on the hour. I can tell him to walk past her door."

Wren speaks before anyone else can, low and quick.

"We've our own place." She swallows. "We can't pay Mother Gannet. I won't have—" She stops and starts again, quieter. "The boathouse is ours."

"Benno's curtain's next to yours," Marrow says. She isn't unkind about it. It's just a fact, set down on the board like the ledger.

Wren doesn't answer that. She looks at James.

Pim says nothing. He's looking at the broken jug on the floor, and his arm is tight across the lid of the tin.

Up on the Rock the bell is quiet. The last bell, when both Gannet's door and the Lower City gate shut, is still a while off. Marrow has stopped talking. She's waiting to hear where the man of the Lady wants these three to sleep.

turns.message:
“Gannet’s. I’ll pay.” I turn to Wren. “One night, while we find help. It doesn’t mean giving up your home, and you owe me nothing.”

To Marrow: “Please leave word at the arch that James Worgen is at Mother Gannet’s with Beshaba-marked coins and people suffering repeated misfortune. Ask the priestess to come before emptying the Lady’s box—if anyone’s put a winning penny in there, she should know what to look for.”

I rise. “Thank you, Sergeant. We’ll tell you what we learn.”

Before we leave, I ask the pie-woman what I owe for the broken jug, and pay it from my own purse. Then I take the others to Gannet’s to arrange rooms before her door shuts.
turns.reply:
James stands up, and Wren's face does what it did when he said yes in the pie-shop. She's braced for something with a hook in it. *One night* and *you owe me nothing* get through to her slowly.

She looks at Pim, at the tin under his forearm, and then at the floor where the jug broke.

"One night." She says it like the terms of a deal, so she'll remember them. "Mother Gannet buys her kindling off the Rivington boy. I'll bring hers for a tenday instead, and she can say no to that if she likes." The last part is for herself, not for James. Her hands let go of the shawl.

Pim talks to his sister as if the man beside him had gone outside. "He's buying beds now." He chews on that and can't find the catch. "Fine. Nobody touches it."

Marrow listens to the message without writing anything down. She'll remember it. At *before she empties the Lady's box* her fork stops over the eel pie.

"Hm."

She thinks for a moment about a winning penny dropped through the slot for luck, sitting all night in the Lady's own box with the other offerings.

"I'll tell the corporal tonight, before he goes off. Worgen, Gannet's, the Maid's mark, folk breaking things. And to look before she empties it." She breaks the crust at last. "Whether she comes is up to her. The Hall doesn't answer to the Fist either."

She doesn't answer his thanks. She nods once at the door and starts on her pie, which is how she says she's done.

The pie-woman has already swept the pieces of the jug into a pile against the oven with the side of her foot. When James asks what he owes, she looks at the pile instead of at him.

"Two copper for the jug. The beer was his, and he'd paid for it." She tips her head at Tobin. James counts two coppers onto the board and they go into the clay pot with the others. "Mind the boy on the step out. It's worn."

Tobin gets up off the bench the way a man gets out of a cold river, a bit at a time. He drops the rag on the table and looks at the jug handle he's still holding. He sets it down carefully next to the rag, like something that might go off.

"Bed with boiled sheets." He rubs his knee. "If I don't go through the floor on the way up, I'll call it a good day." He nearly grins, and it's the first time since the jug.

They step out under the Rock. Torchlight up on the stone, dark river through the gaps in the planks. Pim takes the worn step at the door slowly, testing it with his toe, and doesn't look at anyone while he does it. Three doors up the north span the rope-maker's shop is shuttered for the night, and coils of tarred line hang under the eaves like sleeping bats. Above it is a green door at the top of an outside stair. It's a sturdy stair with new treads, and Pim tries every one of them anyway. A bell hangs on a string beside the door.

James pulls the string. Somewhere inside a small brass bell rings. Bare feet cross a floor, and a hatch the size of a book opens at eye level.

Behind it is a sharp old face in a linen cap tied under the chin. She gives each of them a single look: the cloak and the rapier, the drover with the limp, the kindling girl, the boy with blood dried in his hair, and last of all the cat sitting on the top step.

"Wren," she says, surprised but not unfriendly. Then, to James, because he's the one who rang: "Mother Gannet. You'll be wanting beds, and you'll want them before the bell, same as everybody who comes up my stair at this hour."

The bolt draws back. Inside is a narrow hall that smells sharply of lye and lavender. The floorboards are scrubbed pale and there's a row of boots by the wall.

*Clean,* the cat says through the bond as it crosses the threshold, and sneezes. *Soap. Everything soap.* A pause. *The boy's tin is louder in here. Nothing else to hide behind.*

Mother Gannet holds up a candle and counts off on her fingers.

"Two rooms free. The back one's over the water, two beds and a truckle that pulls out, which'll do for a small one." She glances at Pim. "The front one's a bed and a chair, over the street, noisier. Five silver a room, a silver more for a fire in either. Boots off in the hall. And that boy washes his head in the basin before he goes near my sheets, or he sleeps on the boards."

Pim opens his mouth. Wren puts a hand on his shoulder and he shuts it again.

Mother Gannet waits with the candle, looking at James to see which rooms he wants and how many fires.

"Misfortune." She says it the way she'd say *damp*. She looks at Pim, at the blood dried in his hair and the tin clamped under his arm. Then she looks at Wren, for longer.

"Wren's sold kindling on this bridge since the leaves came down, and she's never once tried to sell me wet sticks." She turns back to James. "Things break in every house, sir. Mostly the lodgers break them. Anything that breaks in my rooms, you pay what it cost me, and I don't want to hear whose fault it was when I name the price."

She lets that settle, then adds, flatly: "Ilse Marrow's been eating her eel under the Rock every night for nine years and she's never sent me trouble yet. If she knows where you are, that'll do."

She sets the candle on the shelf next to the silver and pads off down the hall in her bare feet. A door opens. She comes back with a clay jug in one hand and a glazed washbasin under her arm, puts them down on the floor by the boots, and goes back for something else. This time it's a dented pewter basin and a tin cup, and she carries them into the front room herself.

"Tin dents," she says as she comes out again. "It doesn't crack."

*Tin bowl now. Good. The boy's smell goes in there with him.*

Mother Gannet picks up her candle.

turns.message:
“Fair terms. Thank you.”

I take off my boots and help Tobin with his, then wait while Pim washes before we go upstairs.

At the front room, I ask Pim, “Would you put the closed tin beside the door tonight, rather than in bed with you? Still in your sight, still yours. Just give yourself a little distance from it.”

I point across the landing. “I’ll be right there. If anything breaks, or you need me for any reason, call. You won’t be bothering me.”
turns.reply:
James sets his boots in the row by the wall, beside a pair of fishwife's clogs and somebody's good Sunday shoes. Tobin is still fighting his second boot. He has his bad leg straight out and is trying to reach it without bending the knee. James crouches, gets a hand under the heel and works it off in one long pull.

"Like pulling a calf the wrong way round," Tobin says, grinning at the ceiling. "Only the calf's grateful after." He wiggles his toes in a sock darned so often it's more darn than sock.

Mother Gannet takes Pim into the kitchen. James waits in the hall and hears most of it through the open door. There's water poured from a height. "Head down." A pause. "Lower." Pim says something sullen that gets lost in the splashing. Through the doorway James can see the boy bent over the basin with the tea-tin on the floor between his bare feet, pinned there by both ankles, while Mother Gannet scrubs the dried blood out of his hair with a rag and none of the patience she'd give a sheet. Wren stands just inside the door with a clean cloth over her arm. She doesn't help, because nobody asked her to.

Pim comes out with his hair wet and dark and sticking up. The pink line above his ear shows plainly now that the blood is gone. He has the tin under his arm again before he's finished drying his face.

"Clean," Mother Gannet says, as if she were signing for a delivery, and picks up her candle.

The stair is narrow and steep and it doesn't creak. At the top a small landing has two doors. The left one is open on the front room: one bed under a sloped ceiling, a rush-seated chair, a shuttered window onto the street. In the little grate, kindling that is definitely not Wren's has just caught under a split log, and it throws a moving orange light over everything. The dented pewter basin and the tin cup sit on the windowsill. Nothing in the room would break if you dropped it.

When James asks about the tin, Pim stops dead in the doorway.

He looks at the door, then at the tin, and then he looks at Wren.

"He wants it by the door." His tone makes it sound like a ridiculous idea. "By the door's where people *come in*."

"Pim."

"I'm only saying." He scowls round the room as if it had set him a trick question. Then he crosses to the chair, drags it over the boards to the foot of the bed and turns it so the seat faces the pillow. He puts the tin down on the rush seat, carefully, the way you'd put down an egg, and takes his hands off it. It's about six feet from where his head will be, and nowhere near the door.

"There." He's still talking to Wren. "In my sight. It's not in the bed. That's distance." He sits down on the edge of the mattress with his eyes on the painted lid, as though it might walk off.

Wren looks at the chair, then at James. She doesn't say it's what he asked for. She doesn't say it isn't, either.

Down at James's feet the cat has stopped on the threshold. It doesn't go in.

*Less on him now. A little,* the bond says. *The room has it. The chair has it. The boy still smells of it, like smoke after the fire's out.*

When James points across the landing to the other door, Pim's eyes go there for half a breath, then come back to the tin. He doesn't answer. He doesn't argue, either.

Wren answers for them both. She's standing in the doorway with the clean cloth still over her arm.

"We'll call." She swallows. "If anything breaks." She takes one end of her shawl in her hand and lets it go again. "Goodnight, Mister Worgen."

She shuts the door gently. Through it James hears the chair scrape an inch, Pim's voice low and cross, and then Wren's, lower.

The back room is straight on, over the water, as Mother Gannet said. It has two beds along the walls, a truckle pushed underneath one of them, and a window shuttered against the river. There's no fire, and the boards are cool under James's stocking feet. Under the floor the Chionthar works quietly at the piles. Tobin limps in behind him, looks at the nearer bed, then at the floor, and stamps once on the boards with his good foot to test them. They hold.

"Well," he says. "That's something."

Down in the hall Mother Gannet's candle goes along to the front door. The bolt hasn't gone across yet. The last bell is still a little way off. After that nobody comes up her stair, and nobody goes down it either. Nothing else is waiting on James before then unless he wants it to.

note.text:
The strongest part was how personal the opening became without handing James a quest. The card game tempted him, the cat noticed something wrong, and his decision to investigate led naturally to Wren and Pim. Tymora mattered through his choices rather than through a divine instruction.

**What worked**
- The NPCs felt distinct and grounded. Marrow’s guarded concern, Tobin’s fading jokes, Gannet’s practical kindness, and Pim speaking through his sister all landed.
- Small accidents made the threat unsettling before it became overtly dangerous. Catching Pim on the stairs was the session’s best action moment.
- James could earn trust through concrete acts: supper, healing, lodging, and respecting Pim’s ownership of the tin. Those choices mattered without requiring constant Persuasion rolls.
- Failed Arcana left useful uncertainty instead of stopping the investigation.

**What broke or dragged**
- The pacing became very granular. Cooling a pie, ordering food, arranging beds, washing, and placing the tin each received substantial narration. Individually charming; cumulatively, they crowded out investigation.
- Several turns ended by reiterating that the bell had not rung and everyone was waiting. When I explicitly waited for Marrow, advancing straight to her arrival would have kept momentum.
- The unsolicited out-of-game explanations about the pie and which actions had already happened were distracting. Nothing needed defending or adjudicating there.
- Revealing Dov’s full name before James had learned it was a small viewpoint slip.

**What was missing**
- Clearer distances and remaining time before closing would help me make informed travel decisions.
- I wanted a little more room to test ideas about the coins. The investigation was compelling, but mostly advanced through NPC disclosures while my immediate role became caring for the victims.
- Resource tracking was generally clear, though the initial money conversion and rules discrepancies between the campaign sheet and opening records deserved a brief clarification.

Overall, I cared about these people and wanted to return. Keep the character detail and consequences; compress routine transitions so there’s more room for consequential choices in each session.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."
